How Dominant Were the 2026 Brewers? A Statistical Comparison of MLB Champions, 1969–2026¶

Benji Richheimer · Python · pandas · statsmodels · SciPy · seaborn

On October 28, 2026, the Milwaukee Brewers won the first World Series in franchise history after a 103-59 regular season and an 11-2 postseason. This analysis puts that run in historical context by answering two questions:

  1. Where does the 2026 Brewers' season rank among every World Series champion since 1969?
  2. What, if anything, separates champions from the rest of the playoff field?

Executive summary¶

The 2026 Brewers were a top-10 champion of the divisional era. Their record was fully backed by run differential, and their postseason run ranks #5 of 31 among champions since 1995. They are also an outlier in a league where the regular season does a poor job of predicting October.

Finding Evidence
The 103 wins were earned, not lucky A run-differential model (adj. R² = 0.88, 1,500+ team-seasons) expected 102.5 wins; they won 103
Elite by historical standards #8 of 55 champions in era-adjusted run differential; above the typical champion on 6 of 7 measures
Built on run prevention, not power 4th percentile among champions in home runs per game, one of the least powerful title teams on record
One of the best modern postseason runs 11-2, +2.00 runs per game against opponents with a .595 average record: #5 of 31 champions since 1995
October is mostly noise Regular-season stats explain ~6% of postseason winning %, vs. 88% of regular-season winning %
The best team rarely wins The team with MLB's best record won the title in only 28% of seasons; wild cards and division winners win at statistically similar rates (p = 0.35)

Business takeaway for a front office: run differential is a reliable gauge of true team quality over 162 games, but a short series is close to a coin flip. Roster decisions should be built for regular-season strength, and expectations for any single October should be set with that variance in mind.

1. Data and methodology¶

File Source What it contains
Teams.csv Lahman Baseball Database (SABR), 1871–2025 One row per team per season: wins, losses, runs, runs allowed, ERA, home runs, playoff flags
SeriesPost.csv Lahman One row per playoff series: winner, loser, games won by each
BattingPost.csv, PitchingPost.csv Lahman Every player's postseason runs scored and runs allowed
batting_2026.csv, pitching_2026.csv Baseball-Reference 2026 team batting and pitching tables (Lahman has not added 2026 yet)

Study window: 1969–2026. 1969 is the first season with a playoff round before the World Series, so every team in the sample had to win at least one series to reach it.

Seasons handled separately: 1994 had no postseason because of the players' strike. The 1981 strike-shortened split season and the 60-game 2020 season are excluded from the statistical tests because their unusual formats would distort comparisons with full 162-game seasons.

Era adjustment: scoring environments vary widely across 58 seasons, so every regular-season stat is converted to a z-score against that season's league (Section 2.5). A team two standard deviations above its league in 1972 is directly comparable to one two standard deviations above its league in 2026.

Methods used: independent-samples t-tests (with Bartlett's test for equal variances and Cohen's d), one-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons and eta-squared, OLS regression with out-of-sample prediction, chi-square tests of independence with Cramér's V, Pearson correlation, and percentile and composite-score rankings.

To reproduce: place the six CSV files above in the same folder as this notebook and run all cells. Every analysis is a reusable function, so the Section 5–6 results can be re-run with different stats, groupings, or time windows.

2. Building the dataset¶

2.1 Configuration¶

Every value the code depends on is set here once, so nothing is hard-coded later. TEAM_CODES connects Baseball-Reference's full team names to Lahman's three-letter codes, and the four lists record the 2026 postseason: division winners, wild cards, the two World Series teams, and the champion.

In [ ]:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

DATA_DIR   = "."
START_YEAR = 1969
END_YEAR   = 2026
NEW_SEASON = 2026

# Baseball-Reference uses full team names; Lahman uses 3-letter codes
TEAM_CODES = {
    "Arizona Diamondbacks": "ARI", "Athletics": "ATH",            "Atlanta Braves": "ATL",
    "Baltimore Orioles": "BAL",    "Boston Red Sox": "BOS",       "Chicago Cubs": "CHN",
    "Chicago White Sox": "CHA",    "Cincinnati Reds": "CIN",      "Cleveland Guardians": "CLE",
    "Colorado Rockies": "COL",     "Detroit Tigers": "DET",       "Houston Astros": "HOU",
    "Kansas City Royals": "KCA",   "Los Angeles Angels": "LAA",   "Los Angeles Dodgers": "LAN",
    "Miami Marlins": "MIA",        "Milwaukee Brewers": "MIL",    "Minnesota Twins": "MIN",
    "New York Mets": "NYN",        "New York Yankees": "NYA",     "Philadelphia Phillies": "PHI",
    "Pittsburgh Pirates": "PIT",   "San Diego Padres": "SDN",     "San Francisco Giants": "SFN",
    "Seattle Mariners": "SEA",     "St. Louis Cardinals": "SLN",  "Tampa Bay Rays": "TBA",
    "Texas Rangers": "TEX",        "Toronto Blue Jays": "TOR",    "Washington Nationals": "WAS",
}

# 2026 postseason results (Lahman doesn't have 2026 yet)
DIV_WINNERS_2026 = ["TBA", "CLE", "HOU", "MIL", "LAN", "ATL"]
WILD_CARDS_2026  = ["NYA", "BOS", "CHA", "SDN", "CHN", "PHI"]
PENNANTS_2026    = ["TBA", "MIL"]
CHAMPION_2026    = "MIL"

2.2 Load the Lahman files¶

Read the team and playoff-series tables, and keep only American and National League teams (newer Lahman versions also include Negro Leagues teams).

In [ ]:
teams  = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA_DIR}/Teams.csv")
series = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA_DIR}/SeriesPost.csv")

# keep only AL and NL teams (newer Lahman files also include Negro Leagues teams)
teams = teams[teams["lgID"].isin(["AL", "NL"])]

2.3 Add the 2026 season¶

Lahman stops at 2025, so the 2026 season is built from the two Baseball-Reference tables:

  • Keep only the 30 real teams (this drops the "League Average" and totals rows).
  • The pitching table calls runs allowed "R", so it is renamed to RA before the two tables are merged.
  • Add the columns Lahman has (team code, season, playoff flags) so the 2026 rows can be stacked under 1969–2025.
In [ ]:
bat = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA_DIR}/batting_{NEW_SEASON}.csv")
pit = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA_DIR}/pitching_{NEW_SEASON}.csv")

bat = bat[bat["Tm"].isin(TEAM_CODES)]
pit = pit[pit["Tm"].isin(TEAM_CODES)]

# in the pitching table, "R" means runs ALLOWED
pit = pit.rename(columns={"R": "RA"})
new = pd.merge(bat[["Tm", "R", "HR"]], pit[["Tm", "W", "L", "RA", "ERA"]], on="Tm")

new["name"]   = new["Tm"]
new["teamID"] = new["Tm"].map(TEAM_CODES)
new["yearID"] = NEW_SEASON
# playoff flags, so the 2026 rows match the Lahman columns
new["DivWin"] = np.where(new["teamID"].isin(DIV_WINNERS_2026), "Y", "N")
new["WCWin"]  = np.where(new["teamID"].isin(WILD_CARDS_2026), "Y", "N")
new["LgWin"]  = np.where(new["teamID"].isin(PENNANTS_2026), "Y", "N")
new["WSWin"]  = np.where(new["teamID"] == CHAMPION_2026, "Y", "N")
new = new.drop(columns=["Tm"])

teams = pd.concat([teams, new], ignore_index=True)
teams = teams[(teams["yearID"] >= START_YEAR) & (teams["yearID"] <= END_YEAR)].copy()

2.4 Per-game stats¶

Seasons weren't always 162 games (2020 had only 60), so totals are converted to per-game rates: winning %, run differential per game, and home runs per game.

In [ ]:
# per-game rates, because not every season had 162 games
teams["G"]        = teams["W"] + teams["L"]
teams["win_pct"]  = teams["W"] / teams["G"]
teams["run_diff"] = teams["R"] - teams["RA"]
teams["rd_per_g"] = teams["run_diff"] / teams["G"]
teams["hr_per_g"] = teams["HR"] / teams["G"]

2.5 Z-scores within each season¶

Scoring levels change a lot over time, so each stat is compared with that season's league:

z = (team's value − that season's average) ÷ that season's standard deviation

A z-score of +2.0 means "two standard deviations better than the league that year," whether the season was 1972 or 2026. The z-scores are calculated against all teams in the season, before filtering to playoff teams. For ERA, lower is better, so a negative z-score is good.

In [ ]:
# z = (value - season average) / season std dev, so teams from different eras compare fairly
for col in ["rd_per_g", "win_pct", "ERA", "hr_per_g"]:
    season_mean = teams.groupby("yearID")[col].transform("mean")
    season_std  = teams.groupby("yearID")[col].transform("std")
    teams[col + "_z"] = (teams[col] - season_mean) / season_std

2.6 Keep the playoff teams¶

A team made the playoffs if it appears as a winner or loser in any series in SeriesPost. The 12 playoff teams of 2026 are added from the list in the settings. The result, po, has one row per playoff team per season.

In [ ]:
# every team listed in SeriesPost (as a winner or loser) made the playoffs
winners  = series[["yearID", "teamIDwinner"]].rename(columns={"teamIDwinner": "teamID"})
losers   = series[["yearID", "teamIDloser"]].rename(columns={"teamIDloser": "teamID"})
po_2026  = pd.DataFrame({"yearID": NEW_SEASON, "teamID": DIV_WINNERS_2026 + WILD_CARDS_2026})
playoff_teams = pd.concat([winners, losers, po_2026]).drop_duplicates()

po = pd.merge(teams, playoff_teams, on=["yearID", "teamID"])

2.7 Categorical variables¶

  • outcome – how far the team went: Champion, Lost World Series, or Lost earlier. This means the same thing in every era, even though the number of rounds changed.
  • era – which playoff format the season used, as the field grew from 4 to 12 teams.
  • odd_season – marks 1981 and 2020 so the tests can leave them out.
In [ ]:
def get_outcome(row):
    if row["WSWin"] == "Y":
        return "Champion"
    elif row["LgWin"] == "Y":
        return "Lost World Series"
    else:
        return "Lost earlier"

po["outcome"] = po.apply(get_outcome, axis=1)

# group seasons by playoff format: 4, 8, 10, then 12 teams
po["era"] = pd.cut(po["yearID"],
                   bins=[1968, 1993, 2011, 2021, END_YEAR],
                   labels=["1969-93 (4 teams)", "1995-2011 (8 teams)", "2012-21 (10 teams)", "2022+ (12 teams)"])

# 1981 (split season) and 2020 (60 games) are left out of the tests
po["odd_season"] = po["yearID"].isin([1981, 2020])

There should be 406 playoff team-seasons, including 57 champions and 57 World Series losers, and the 2026 table should show the Brewers as Champion and the Rays as Lost World Series.

3. Building postseason records¶

Lahman stores the postseason in separate tables, none of which has one row per team. This section reshapes and combines them into one row per team per postseason.

3.1 One row per team per series¶

Each series is split into two rows – one from the winner's side and one from the loser's – so every team gets its own games won, games lost, and opponent. The Brewers' three 2026 series are entered by hand: 3-1 over San Diego, 4-0 over the Dodgers, and 4-1 over Tampa Bay.

In [ ]:
# one row per team per series: the winner's side and the loser's side
winner_rows = series.rename(columns={"teamIDwinner": "teamID", "teamIDloser": "opponent",
                                     "wins": "g_won", "losses": "g_lost"})
loser_rows  = series.rename(columns={"teamIDloser": "teamID", "teamIDwinner": "opponent",
                                     "losses": "g_won", "wins": "g_lost"})
cols = ["yearID", "teamID", "opponent", "g_won", "g_lost"]
team_series = pd.concat([winner_rows[cols], loser_rows[cols]])

# 2026 isn't in Lahman yet: Brewers beat SD 3-1, LAD 4-0, TB 4-1
brewers_2026 = pd.DataFrame({
    "yearID":   [2026, 2026, 2026],
    "teamID":   ["MIL", "MIL", "MIL"],
    "opponent": ["SDN", "LAN", "TBA"],
    "g_won":    [3, 4, 4],
    "g_lost":   [1, 0, 1],
})
team_series = pd.concat([team_series, brewers_2026])

3.2 Opponent strength and postseason winning %¶

Each opponent's regular-season winning % is looked up and averaged, which measures how tough a team's path was. Games are then added up into each team's full postseason record.

In [ ]:
# look up each opponent's regular-season W% to measure how tough the path was
opponents = teams[["yearID", "teamID", "win_pct"]].rename(columns={"teamID": "opponent", "win_pct": "opp_wpct"})
team_series = pd.merge(team_series, opponents, on=["yearID", "opponent"], how="left")

post = team_series.groupby(["yearID", "teamID"]).agg({"g_won": "sum", "g_lost": "sum", "opp_wpct": "mean"})
post = post.reset_index()
post["post_wpct"] = post["g_won"] / (post["g_won"] + post["g_lost"])

3.3 Postseason runs and margin¶

Every player's postseason runs scored (BattingPost) and runs allowed (PitchingPost) are summed by team. The 2026 Brewers outscored their opponents 59-33. Average margin = (runs scored − runs allowed) ÷ games played. Lahman has no game-by-game scores, so this is the average across all postseason games, not just wins.

In [ ]:
bat_post = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA_DIR}/BattingPost.csv")
pit_post = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA_DIR}/PitchingPost.csv")
# add up every player's postseason runs to get team runs scored and allowed
runs_for     = bat_post.groupby(["yearID", "teamID"])["R"].sum().reset_index().rename(columns={"R": "post_runs"})
runs_against = pit_post.groupby(["yearID", "teamID"])["R"].sum().reset_index().rename(columns={"R": "post_runs_allowed"})
runs = pd.merge(runs_for, runs_against, on=["yearID", "teamID"])

# 2026 Brewers outscored their opponents 59-33
runs = pd.concat([runs, pd.DataFrame({"yearID": [2026], "teamID": ["MIL"],
                                      "post_runs": [59], "post_runs_allowed": [33]})])

post = pd.merge(post, runs, on=["yearID", "teamID"], how="left")
# average run margin per postseason game
post["post_margin"] = (post["post_runs"] - post["post_runs_allowed"]) / (post["g_won"] + post["g_lost"])

3.4 Attach to the playoff-team table¶

The table shows the most recent champions as a check. The last row should be the 2026 Brewers: 11-2, .846, opponents .595, +2.00 runs per game.

In [ ]:
po = pd.merge(po, post, on=["yearID", "teamID"], how="left")

4. Analysis helpers¶

Shared settings and utilities used by every analysis, so no logic is repeated:

  • STATS – the four stats a user can pick, with readable names and whether a higher number is better.
  • analysis – the playoff teams used in the tests (1981 and 2020 removed). brewers_row – the 2026 Brewers' data, used to mark them with a star on the charts.
  • pick() – handles every sub-choice: lists numbered options and asks the user to choose. When a choice is passed in as an argument, it skips the prompt, so every analysis can run interactively or as a plain function call.
  • p_sentence() – turns a p-value into a plain-language interpretation.
  • size_label() – labels an effect size as negligible, small, medium, or large.
  • styled() – shows a results table with a title and rounded numbers.
In [ ]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.formula.api import ols
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
ALPHA = 0.05
BREWERS = (NEW_SEASON, "MIL")

STATS = {
    "rd_per_g_z": ("Run differential per game (z vs. league)", True),
    "win_pct_z":  ("Winning % (z vs. league)",                 True),
    "ERA_z":      ("Team ERA (z vs. league)",                  False),
    "hr_per_g_z": ("Home runs per game (z vs. league)",        True),
}

# leave out 1981 and 2020 for the statistical tests
analysis = po[po["odd_season"] == False].copy()

brewers_row = po[(po["yearID"] == BREWERS[0]) & (po["teamID"] == BREWERS[1])].iloc[0]

def get_label(value):
    """Option values are either a label, or a tuple whose first item is the label."""
    if isinstance(value, tuple):
        return value[0]
    return value

def pick(options, prompt, choice=None):
    """Sub-choice menu: list the options, ask for a number, return the matching key.
    If a choice is passed in as an argument, skip the prompt."""
    if choice is not None:
        return choice
    keys = list(options.keys())
    for number, key in enumerate(keys, start=1):
        print(f"  {number}. {get_label(options[key])}")
    while True:
        answer = input(prompt)
        if answer.isdigit() and 1 <= int(answer) <= len(keys):
            return keys[int(answer) - 1]
        print("  Please enter one of the numbers above.")

def p_sentence(p, what):
    """Plain-language interpretation of a p-value."""
    if p < 0.001:
        p_text = "p < 0.001"
    else:
        p_text = f"p = {p:.3f}"
    confidence = f"{1 - ALPHA:.0%}"
    if p < ALPHA:
        return f"The result ({p_text}) suggests a statistically significant {what} at the {confidence} confidence level."
    else:
        return f"The result ({p_text}) does not show a statistically significant {what} at the {confidence} confidence level."

def size_label(value, cutoffs):
    """Label an effect size using (small, medium, large) cutoffs."""
    small, medium, large = cutoffs
    value = abs(value)
    if value < small:
        return "negligible"
    elif value < medium:
        return "small"
    elif value < large:
        return "medium"
    else:
        return "large"

def styled(df, title, fmt="{:.3f}"):
    """Show a results table with a title and rounded numbers."""
    display(df.style.format(fmt).set_caption(title))

5. How good were the 2026 Brewers?¶

Three angles: how they compare with every champion on regular-season and postseason measures (5.1), whether their record was backed by run differential (5.2), and how their postseason run ranks on its own (5.3).

5.1 The 2026 Brewers vs. every champion since 1969¶

Question: Where do the Brewers rank among all champions since 1969?

Method: a percentile for each stat (the % of other champions the Brewers matched or beat; for ERA, lower is better), plus a top-10 table with the Brewers highlighted in gold – added at the bottom if they rank outside the top 10.

Parameters: stat – which measure to rank the top 10 by; summary=False shows only the top-10 table.

In [ ]:
COMPARE = {
    "rd_per_g_z":  ("Run differential per game (z vs. league)", True),
    "win_pct_z":   ("Winning % (z vs. league)", True),
    "ERA_z":       ("Team ERA (z vs. league)", False),
    "hr_per_g_z":  ("Home runs per game (z vs. league)", True),
    "post_wpct":   ("Postseason winning %", True),
    "post_margin": ("Postseason run margin per game", True),
    "opp_wpct":    ("Opponents' regular-season winning %", True),
}

def highlight_brewers(row):
    """Color the 2026 Brewers' row gold in the top-10 table."""
    if row["Season"] == NEW_SEASON:
        return ["background-color: gold; color: black; font-weight: bold"] * len(row)
    return [""] * len(row)

def run_brewers(stat=None, summary=True):
    stat = pick(COMPARE, "Rank the champions by: ", stat)
    label, higher_better = COMPARE[stat]

    champs = analysis[analysis["outcome"] == "Champion"].copy()
    others = champs[champs["yearID"] != NEW_SEASON]

    if summary:
        rows = []
        for col in COMPARE:
            name, hb = COMPARE[col]
            values = others[col].dropna()
            brewers_value = brewers_row[col]
            # percentile = share of other champions the Brewers matched or beat (for ERA, lower is better)
            if hb:
                percentile = (values <= brewers_value).mean() * 100
            else:
                percentile = (values >= brewers_value).mean() * 100
            rows.append([name.split(" (")[0], brewers_value, values.median(), percentile])
        pct_table = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Stat", "2026 Brewers", "Champions' median", "Percentile"])
        pct_table = pct_table.set_index("Stat")
        styled(pct_table, f"2026 Brewers vs. {len(others)} other champions ({START_YEAR}–{NEW_SEASON - 1})",
               {"2026 Brewers": "{:+.3f}", "Champions' median": "{:+.3f}", "Percentile": "{:.0f}"})

    ranked = champs.dropna(subset=[stat]).sort_values(stat, ascending=not higher_better)
    ranked["Rank"] = range(1, len(ranked) + 1)
    brewers_rank = ranked[ranked["yearID"] == NEW_SEASON]["Rank"].iloc[0]

    top10 = ranked.head(10)
    if brewers_rank > 10:
        top10 = pd.concat([top10, ranked[ranked["yearID"] == NEW_SEASON]])
    top10 = top10[["Rank", "yearID", "name", "W", "L", stat]]
    top10 = top10.rename(columns={"yearID": "Season", "name": "Team", stat: label})
    display(top10.style.hide(axis="index")
                 .format({label: "{:+.3f}"})
                 .apply(highlight_brewers, axis=1)
                 .set_caption(f"Top 10 champions by {label} – the 2026 Brewers rank #{brewers_rank} of {len(ranked)}"))

    if summary:
        plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
        colors = ["gold" if v >= 50 else "navy" for v in pct_table["Percentile"]]
        plt.barh(pct_table.index, pct_table["Percentile"], color=colors, edgecolor="black",
                 label="Brewers' percentile among champions")
        for i, value in enumerate(pct_table["Percentile"]):
            plt.text(value + 1, i, f"{value:.0f}th", va="center")
        plt.axvline(50, color="red", linestyle="--", label="Typical champion (50th)")
        plt.xlim(0, 110)
        plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
        plt.title(f"Where the 2026 Brewers Rank Among {len(others)} World Series Champions Since {START_YEAR}")
        plt.xlabel("Percentile (100 = as good as or better than every other champion)")
        plt.ylabel("Stat")
        plt.legend(loc="lower right")
        plt.show()

    text = (f"**Interpretation:** On **{label.split(' (')[0].lower()}**, the 2026 Brewers rank "
            f"**#{brewers_rank} of {len(ranked)}** champions since {START_YEAR}.")
    if summary:
        strongest = pct_table["Percentile"].idxmax()
        weakest = pct_table["Percentile"].idxmin()
        above = (pct_table["Percentile"] > 50).sum()
        text += (f" They beat the typical champion on **{above} of {len(pct_table)}** measures. "
                 f"Their strongest category is **{strongest.lower()}** ({pct_table.loc[strongest, 'Percentile']:.0f}th percentile) "
                 f"and their weakest is **{weakest.lower()}** ({pct_table.loc[weakest, 'Percentile']:.0f}th). "
                 f"Regular-season stats are z-scores against each season's league; postseason stats are raw values.")
    display(Markdown(text))

5.2 Was the 103-win season earned?¶

Question: Did the Brewers win as many games as their run differential says they should have, or did they get lucky in close games?

Method: OLS regression of winning % on run differential per game for every MLB team from 1969 to 2025 (strike-shortened 1981 and 2020 excluded). The 2026 Brewers are held out of the training data and scored with the fitted model. Teams far above the regression line won more games than their run differential supports, which usually reflects luck. A residual table identifies the luckiest and unluckiest teams of the era.

In [ ]:
REG_QUESTIONS = {
    "earned":  "Was the Brewers' 103-win season earned? (run differential -> winning %)",
    "october": "Can the regular season predict October? (regular-season stats -> postseason winning %)",
}
MODELS = {
    "m1": ("Run differential only", "post_wpct ~ rd_per_g_z"),
    "m2": ("Run differential + ERA + HR", "post_wpct ~ rd_per_g_z + ERA_z + hr_per_g_z"),
    "m3": ("Run differential + ERA + HR + playoff era", "post_wpct ~ rd_per_g_z + ERA_z + hr_per_g_z + era"),
}
SEASON_GAMES = 162

all_teams = teams[teams["yearID"] < NEW_SEASON]
all_teams = all_teams[(all_teams["yearID"] != 1981) & (all_teams["yearID"] != 2020)]
train = analysis[analysis["yearID"] < NEW_SEASON].dropna(subset=["post_wpct"])
brewers_all = teams[(teams["yearID"] == NEW_SEASON) & (teams["teamID"] == "MIL")]


def fmt_p(p):
    """Show tiny p-values as '< 0.0001' instead of 0.0000."""
    if p < 0.0001:
        return "< 0.0001"
    return f"{p:.4f}"


def reg_equation(model, y_name):
    """Build a readable regression equation string from the fitted coefficients."""
    coefs = model.params
    equation = f"{y_name} = {coefs.iloc[0]:.3f}"
    for name in coefs.index[1:]:
        equation += f" + {coefs[name]:.3f} {name}"
    return equation.replace("+ -", "- ")


def coef_table(model, title):
    """Coefficient table with p-values and 95% confidence intervals."""
    ci = model.conf_int(alpha=ALPHA)
    table = pd.DataFrame({"Coefficient": model.params, "p-value": model.pvalues,
                          "95% CI low": ci[0], "95% CI high": ci[1]})
    styled(table, title, {"Coefficient": "{:.4f}", "p-value": fmt_p,
                          "95% CI low": "{:.4f}", "95% CI high": "{:.4f}"})


def regression_earned():
    model = ols("win_pct ~ rd_per_g", data=all_teams).fit()
    slope = model.params["rd_per_g"]
    coef_table(model, f"Question A: Winning % ~ run differential per game (n = {int(model.nobs)} team-seasons)")

    results = all_teams[["yearID", "name", "W", "L"]].copy()
    # expected wins = predicted winning % x games played
    results["Expected W"] = model.predict(all_teams) * all_teams["G"]
    results["Wins above expected"] = results["W"] - results["Expected W"]
    luck = pd.concat([results.sort_values("Wins above expected", ascending=False).head(5),
                      results.sort_values("Wins above expected").head(5)])
    luck = luck.rename(columns={"yearID": "Season", "name": "Team"}).set_index(["Season", "Team"])
    styled(luck, "Luckiest and unluckiest teams since 1969 (actual wins vs. wins expected from run differential)",
           {"W": "{:.0f}", "L": "{:.0f}", "Expected W": "{:.1f}", "Wins above expected": "{:+.1f}"})

    expected_w = model.predict(brewers_all).iloc[0] * SEASON_GAMES
    actual_w = brewers_all["W"].iloc[0]

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    plt.scatter(all_teams["rd_per_g"], all_teams["win_pct"], s=8, alpha=0.3, label="MLB teams 1969–2025")
    plt.plot(all_teams["rd_per_g"], model.predict(all_teams), color="red", linewidth=2, label="Regression line")
    plt.scatter(brewers_all["rd_per_g"], brewers_all["win_pct"], marker="*", s=450, color="gold",
                edgecolor="black", zorder=5, label=f"2026 Brewers: {actual_w:.0f} W (expected {expected_w:.1f})")
    plt.title(f"Run Differential Explains Regular-Season Winning\n"
              f"{reg_equation(model, 'Win%')}   |   Adjusted R-Squared = {model.rsquared_adj:.3f}, "
              f"p-value {fmt_p(model.f_pvalue)}")
    plt.xlabel("Run differential per game")
    plt.ylabel("Winning %")
    plt.legend(loc="upper left")
    plt.show()

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
    plt.scatter(model.predict(all_teams), model.resid * SEASON_GAMES, s=8, alpha=0.3, label="Each team")
    plt.axhline(0, color="red", linewidth=2, label="Exactly as expected")
    plt.title("Residuals: Wins Above or Below Expected\n"
              "(a good model shows dots spread evenly around 0, with no pattern)")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted winning %")
    plt.ylabel("Residual (wins per 162 games)")
    plt.legend(loc="upper left")
    plt.show()

    gap = actual_w - expected_w
    if abs(gap) < 3:
        verdict = "earned, not lucky"
    elif gap > 0:
        verdict = "a bit lucky"
    else:
        verdict = "a bit unlucky"
    display(Markdown(
        f"**Equation:** `{reg_equation(model, 'Win%')}`\n\n"
        f"**Interpretation:** {p_sentence(model.f_pvalue, 'relationship between run differential and winning %')} "
        f"The Adjusted R-Squared of {model.rsquared_adj:.3f} means run differential explains about "
        f"**{model.rsquared_adj:.0%}** of the differences in teams' winning %. Each extra run of differential per game "
        f"is worth about **{slope * SEASON_GAMES:.1f} wins** over a 162-game season. The model expected the 2026 Brewers "
        f"to win **{expected_w:.1f}** games; they won **{actual_w:.0f}**, so their record was **{verdict}** "
        f"({gap:+.1f} wins vs. expected)."
    ))

5.3 Ranking the 2026 postseason run¶

Question: Where does the Brewers' postseason run rank among all champions' runs?

Method: a single postseason score – the average of three z-scores among champions: postseason winning %, run margin per game, and opponents' regular-season winning %.

It can be run two ways: all champions since 1969, or only since 1995. The 1995 version is the fairer comparison: before 1995 a champion needed only 7–8 postseason wins, so short sweeps inflate older teams' numbers, while every champion since 1995 had to win at least three series.

In [ ]:
POST_STATS = {
    "post_wpct":   "Postseason W%",
    "post_margin": "Run margin per game",
    "opp_wpct":    "Opponents' W%",
}

def rank_postseason_runs(start_year=START_YEAR):
    champs = analysis[(analysis["outcome"] == "Champion") & (analysis["yearID"] >= start_year)].copy()

    # z-score each stat among champions, then average the three into one score
    for col in POST_STATS:
        champs[col + "_score"] = (champs[col] - champs[col].mean()) / champs[col].std()
    champs["Postseason score"] = champs[[col + "_score" for col in POST_STATS]].mean(axis=1)

    champs = champs.sort_values("Postseason score", ascending=False)
    champs["Rank"] = range(1, len(champs) + 1)
    brewers_rank = champs[champs["yearID"] == NEW_SEASON]["Rank"].iloc[0]

    table = champs.head(10).copy()
    if brewers_rank > 10:
        table = pd.concat([table, champs[champs["yearID"] == NEW_SEASON]])
    table["Record"] = table["g_won"].astype(int).astype(str) + "-" + table["g_lost"].astype(int).astype(str)
    table = table[["Rank", "yearID", "name", "Record"] + list(POST_STATS) + ["Postseason score"]]
    table = table.rename(columns={"yearID": "Season", "name": "Team", **POST_STATS})
    display(table.style.hide(axis="index")
                 .format({"Postseason W%": "{:.3f}", "Run margin per game": "{:+.2f}",
                          "Opponents' W%": "{:.3f}", "Postseason score": "{:+.2f}"})
                 .apply(highlight_brewers, axis=1)
                 .set_caption(f"Best postseason runs by a champion, {start_year}–{NEW_SEASON} – "
                              f"the 2026 Brewers rank #{brewers_rank} of {len(champs)}"))

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
    colors = ["gold" if y == NEW_SEASON else "lightsteelblue" for y in champs["yearID"]]
    plt.bar(range(1, len(champs) + 1), champs["Postseason score"], color=colors, edgecolor="gray")
    plt.bar(brewers_rank, champs[champs["yearID"] == NEW_SEASON]["Postseason score"],
            color="gold", edgecolor="black", label=f"2026 Brewers (#{brewers_rank})")
    plt.axhline(0, color="red", linestyle="--", label="Average champion")
    plt.title(f"Postseason Runs of Every Champion, {start_year}–{NEW_SEASON}, Ranked Best to Worst")
    plt.xlabel("Rank")
    plt.ylabel("Postseason score (average z-score)")
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

    pct = (champs["Postseason score"] < champs[champs["yearID"] == NEW_SEASON]["Postseason score"].iloc[0]).mean()
    display(Markdown(
        f"**Interpretation:** Combining postseason winning %, run margin, and opponent strength, the 2026 Brewers' "
        f"run ranks **#{brewers_rank} of {len(champs)}** champions since {start_year} – better than **{pct:.0%}** of them. "
        f"A score of 0 is an average champion's run; each point is one standard deviation better."
    ))

6. What separates champions from the field?¶

With the Brewers placed in context, this section asks the broader question: can regular-season performance tell you who will win in October?

6.1 Are champions better than other playoff teams? (t-test)¶

Question: Do champions have better regular-season numbers than the other playoff teams?

Method: a Bartlett test checks whether the two groups have equal variances, and its result decides which t-test to run – the standard two-sample t-test or Welch's t-test. Cohen's d measures how big the difference is (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large).

Parameters: stat – which of the four stats to compare. Output: group summary, Bartlett and t-test tables, a box plot with the 2026 Brewers marked, and an interpretation.

In [ ]:
def run_ttest(stat=None):
    stat = pick(STATS, "Which stat do you want to compare? ", stat)
    label, higher_better = STATS[stat]

    champs = analysis[analysis["outcome"] == "Champion"][stat].dropna()
    others = analysis[analysis["outcome"] != "Champion"][stat].dropna()

    # Bartlett test decides which t-test to run (equal vs. unequal variances)
    b_stat, b_p = stats.bartlett(champs, others)
    equal_var = b_p >= ALPHA
    if equal_var:
        test_name = "Two-sample t-test (equal variances)"
    else:
        test_name = "Welch's t-test (unequal variances)"

    result = stats.ttest_ind(champs, others, equal_var=equal_var)
    t, p = result.statistic, result.pvalue
    ci = result.confidence_interval(confidence_level=1 - ALPHA)

    diff = champs.mean() - others.mean()
    n1, n2 = len(champs), len(others)
    # Cohen's d = difference in means / pooled standard deviation
    pooled_sd = np.sqrt(((n1 - 1) * champs.var() + (n2 - 1) * others.var()) / (n1 + n2 - 2))
    d = diff / pooled_sd

    summary = pd.DataFrame({"n": [n1, n2],
                            "Mean": [champs.mean(), others.mean()],
                            "Std Dev": [champs.std(), others.std()]},
                           index=["Champions", "Other playoff teams"])
    styled(summary, f"Group summary: {label}", {"n": "{:.0f}", "Mean": "{:.3f}", "Std Dev": "{:.3f}"})

    var_test = pd.DataFrame({"Statistic": [b_stat], "p-value": [b_p]}, index=["Bartlett test"])
    styled(var_test, "Step 1: Test for equal variances", {"Statistic": "{:.3f}", "p-value": "{:.4f}"})

    t_table = pd.DataFrame({"t": [t], "df": [result.df], "p-value": [p], "Mean diff": [diff],
                            "95% CI low": [ci.low], "95% CI high": [ci.high], "Cohen's d": [d]},
                           index=[test_name])
    styled(t_table, "Step 2: Independent samples t-test",
           {"t": "{:.3f}", "df": "{:.1f}", "p-value": "{:.4f}", "Mean diff": "{:.3f}",
            "95% CI low": "{:.3f}", "95% CI high": "{:.3f}", "Cohen's d": "{:.3f}"})

    plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
    plt.boxplot([champs, others])
    plt.xticks([1, 2], [f"Champions\n(mean {champs.mean():+.2f})",
                        f"Other playoff teams\n(mean {others.mean():+.2f})"])
    plt.scatter(1, brewers_row[stat], marker="*", s=350, color="gold", edgecolor="black",
                zorder=5, label="2026 Brewers")
    plt.axhline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--", label="League average")
    plt.title(f"{label}: Champions vs. Other Playoff Teams\n{test_name}: t = {t:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}, d = {d:.2f}")
    plt.ylabel(label)
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

    short = label.split(" (")[0]
    if p < ALPHA:
        if (diff > 0) == higher_better:
            takeaway = f"Champions were **better** in {short} on average – but strength in this stat helps, it doesn't guarantee a title."
        else:
            takeaway = f"Champions were **worse** in {short} on average."
    else:
        takeaway = f"{short} doesn't separate champions from the rest of the playoff field."

    display(Markdown(
        f"**Interpretation:** {p_sentence(p, 'difference between champions and other playoff teams')} "
        f"Champions averaged {champs.mean():+.2f} and other playoff teams {others.mean():+.2f} "
        f"standard deviations from their league's average. "
        f"Cohen's d = {d:.2f} is a **{size_label(d, (0.2, 0.5, 0.8))}** effect. {takeaway}"
    ))

6.2 Do outcomes or eras differ? (one-way ANOVA)¶

Question: Do groups of teams differ on a stat? Two groupings are available:

  • Playoff outcome – champions vs. World Series losers vs. teams that lost earlier.
  • Playoff era (champions only) – have title teams gotten weaker or stronger as the playoffs grew from 4 to 12 teams?

Method: f_oneway tests whether any group mean differs; Tukey HSD shows which pairs differ, with plot_simultaneous and a red line at the overall mean. Eta-squared is the share of variation explained by the groups.

Parameters: group_col (outcome or era) and stat.

In [ ]:
GROUPINGS = {
    "outcome": ("Playoff outcome (Champion / Lost World Series / Lost earlier)",
                ["Champion", "Lost World Series", "Lost earlier"]),
    "era":     ("Playoff era (champions only – as the playoffs grew from 4 to 12 teams)",
                ["1969-93 (4 teams)", "1995-2011 (8 teams)", "2012-21 (10 teams)", "2022+ (12 teams)"]),
}

def run_anova(group_col=None, stat=None):
    group_col = pick(GROUPINGS, "Group teams by: ", group_col)
    stat = pick(STATS, "Which stat? ", stat)
    group_names = GROUPINGS[group_col][1]
    label, higher_better = STATS[stat]
    short = label.split(" (")[0].lower()

    data = analysis.dropna(subset=[stat])
    if group_col == "era":
        data = data[data["outcome"] == "Champion"]

    groups = []
    for name in group_names:
        groups.append(data[data[group_col] == name][stat])

    f, p = stats.f_oneway(*groups)

    # eta-squared = between-group variation / total variation
    overall_mean = data[stat].mean()
    ss_between = 0
    for g in groups:
        ss_between += len(g) * (g.mean() - overall_mean) ** 2
    ss_total = ((data[stat] - overall_mean) ** 2).sum()
    eta_sq = ss_between / ss_total

    summary = pd.DataFrame({"n": [len(g) for g in groups],
                            "Mean": [g.mean() for g in groups],
                            "Std Dev": [g.std() for g in groups]},
                           index=group_names)
    styled(summary, f"{label} by {group_col}", {"n": "{:.0f}", "Mean": "{:.3f}", "Std Dev": "{:.3f}"})

    anova_table = pd.DataFrame({"F": [f], "p-value": [p], "Eta-squared": [eta_sq]}, index=["One-way ANOVA"])
    styled(anova_table, "One-way ANOVA results", {"F": "{:.3f}", "p-value": "{:.4f}", "Eta-squared": "{:.3f}"})

    # Tukey HSD shows which pairs of groups differ
    tukey = pairwise_tukeyhsd(endog=data[stat], groups=data[group_col].astype(str), alpha=ALPHA)
    rows = tukey.summary().data
    tukey_table = pd.DataFrame(rows[1:], columns=rows[0])
    display(tukey_table.style.hide(axis="index").set_caption("Step 3: Tukey HSD multiple comparisons"))

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
    plt.boxplot(groups)
    plt.xticks(range(1, len(group_names) + 1),
               [f"{name}\n(mean {g.mean():+.2f})" for name, g in zip(group_names, groups)], fontsize=9)
    brewers_position = group_names.index(brewers_row[group_col]) + 1
    plt.scatter(brewers_position, brewers_row[stat], marker="*", s=350, color="gold",
                edgecolor="black", zorder=5, label="2026 Brewers")
    plt.axhline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--", label="League average")
    plt.title(f"{label} by {group_col.title()}\nF = {f:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}, eta² = {eta_sq:.3f}")
    plt.ylabel(label)
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

    tukey.plot_simultaneous(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.axvline(overall_mean, color="red", label=f"Overall mean ({overall_mean:.2f})")
    plt.title("Tukey HSD: 95% confidence interval for each group\n(groups whose intervals don't overlap are different)")
    plt.xlabel(label)
    plt.ylabel(group_col.title())
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

    different = tukey_table[tukey_table["reject"] == True]
    if len(different) > 0:
        pairs = "; ".join(different["group1"] + " vs. " + different["group2"])
        pair_text = f"Tukey's test found these pairs differ: {pairs}."
    else:
        pair_text = "Tukey's test found no pair of groups that differs significantly."

    if higher_better:
        best = summary["Mean"].idxmax()
    else:
        best = summary["Mean"].idxmin()

    caution = "" if p < ALPHA else " Because the ANOVA isn't significant, these differences could be due to chance."
    display(Markdown(
        f"**Interpretation:** {p_sentence(p, f'difference in {short} across groups')} {pair_text} "
        f"The best average was **{best}** ({summary.loc[best, 'Mean']:+.2f}). "
        f"Eta-squared = {eta_sq:.3f}, so the grouping explains about **{eta_sq:.1%}** of the variation "
        f"({size_label(eta_sq, (0.01, 0.06, 0.14))} effect).{caution}"
    ))

6.3 Can the regular season predict October? (regression)¶

Question: How much of a team's postseason winning % can be explained by its regular-season profile?

Method: three nested OLS models of postseason winning % for playoff teams from 1969 to 2025 – run differential alone; plus ERA and home runs; plus playoff era – compared on adjusted R². The selected model is then used to predict the held-out 2026 Brewers. The low R² compared with Section 5.2 is the central result: the same stats that explain the regular season explain very little of the postseason.

Parameters: model_key – m1, m2, or m3.

In [ ]:
def regression_october(model_key=None):
    model_key = pick(MODELS, "Which model? ", model_key)
    title, formula = MODELS[model_key]

    comparison = []
    for key in MODELS:
        m = ols(MODELS[key][1], data=train).fit()
        comparison.append([MODELS[key][0], m.rsquared_adj, m.f_pvalue, int(m.nobs)])
    comparison = pd.DataFrame(comparison, columns=["Model", "Adjusted R-Squared", "p-value", "n"]).set_index("Model")
    styled(comparison, "Question B: model comparison (1969–2025 playoff teams)",
           {"Adjusted R-Squared": "{:.3f}", "p-value": fmt_p, "n": "{:.0f}"})

    model = ols(formula, data=train).fit()
    coef_table(model, f"Selected model: {title}")

    predicted = model.predict(pd.DataFrame([brewers_row])).iloc[0]
    actual = brewers_row["post_wpct"]
    # share of playoff teams whose residual was smaller than the Brewers'
    share_beaten = (model.resid < actual - predicted).mean()

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    plt.scatter(train["post_wpct"], model.predict(train), s=20, alpha=0.4, label="Playoff teams 1969–2025")
    plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="red", linewidth=2, label="Perfect prediction")
    plt.scatter(actual, predicted, marker="*", s=450, color="gold", edgecolor="black", zorder=5,
                label=f"2026 Brewers (actual {actual:.3f}, predicted {predicted:.3f})")
    plt.title(f"Actual vs. Predicted Postseason Winning % – {title}\n"
              f"Adjusted R-Squared = {model.rsquared_adj:.3f}, p-value {fmt_p(model.f_pvalue)}")
    plt.xlabel("Actual postseason winning %")
    plt.ylabel("Predicted postseason winning %")
    plt.legend(loc="upper left")
    plt.show()

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
    plt.scatter(model.predict(train), model.resid, s=20, alpha=0.4, label="Each playoff team")
    plt.axhline(0, color="red", linewidth=2, label="No error")
    plt.title("Residuals vs. Predicted Postseason Winning %\n"
              "(diagonal stripes appear because a short postseason allows only a few W% values)")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted postseason winning %")
    plt.ylabel("Residual (actual – predicted)")
    plt.legend(loc="upper left")
    plt.show()

    significant = [name for name in model.pvalues.index[1:] if model.pvalues[name] < ALPHA]
    if significant:
        sig_text = "Significant predictors: " + ", ".join(significant) + "."
    else:
        sig_text = "No individual predictor is significant."
    earned_r2 = ols("win_pct ~ rd_per_g", data=all_teams).fit().rsquared_adj

    display(Markdown(
        f"**Equation:** `{reg_equation(model, 'Postseason W%')}`\n\n"
        f"**Interpretation:** {p_sentence(model.f_pvalue, 'relationship between regular-season stats and postseason winning %')} "
        f"But the Adjusted R-Squared of {model.rsquared_adj:.3f} means these stats explain only about "
        f"**{model.rsquared_adj:.0%}** of the differences in postseason winning % – compared with **{earned_r2:.0%}** "
        f"for run differential in the regular season (Question A). {sig_text} With so few games, October results are "
        f"mostly noise. The model predicted the 2026 Brewers at **{predicted:.3f}**; they played **{actual:.3f}**, "
        f"beating the prediction by more than **{share_beaten:.0%}** of playoff teams since 1969."
    ))


def run_regression(question=None, model_key=None):
    question = pick(REG_QUESTIONS, "Which question? ", question)
    if question == "earned":
        regression_earned()
    else:
        regression_october(model_key)

6.4 Which stats move with postseason success? (correlation)¶

Question: Which regular-season stats move together with postseason success?

Method: .corr() for every pair of variables, with significance stars from stats.pearsonr (* p < .05, ** p < .01, *** p < .001). Only the lower half is shown, because the upper half is a mirror image.

Parameters: era_choice – all eras, or a single playoff era.

In [ ]:
CORR_VARS = {
    "rd_per_g_z":  "Run differential per game",
    "win_pct_z":   "Winning %",
    "ERA_z":       "Team ERA",
    "hr_per_g_z":  "Home runs per game",
    "opp_wpct":    "Opponent W%",
    "post_margin": "Postseason margin",
    "post_wpct":   "Postseason W%",
    "is_champ":    "Won title (1 = yes)",
}
ERA_CHOICES = {
    "all":                 "All eras",
    "1969-93 (4 teams)":   "1969-93 (4 teams)",
    "1995-2011 (8 teams)": "1995-2011 (8 teams)",
    "2012-21 (10 teams)":  "2012-21 (10 teams)",
    "2022+ (12 teams)":    "2022+ (12 teams)",
}

def strength(r):
    """Describe how strong a correlation is."""
    if abs(r) < 0.3:
        return "weak"
    elif abs(r) < 0.5:
        return "moderate"
    else:
        return "strong"

def run_corr(era_choice=None):
    era_choice = pick(ERA_CHOICES, "Which era? ", era_choice)

    data = analysis[analysis["yearID"] < NEW_SEASON].copy()
    data["is_champ"] = np.where(data["outcome"] == "Champion", 1, 0)
    if era_choice != "all":
        data = data[data["era"] == era_choice]
    data = data[list(CORR_VARS.keys())].dropna().rename(columns=CORR_VARS)

    corr = data.corr()

    labels = corr.copy().astype(str)
    for row in corr.index:
        for col in corr.columns:
            r, p = stats.pearsonr(data[row], data[col])
            if p < 0.001:
                stars = "***"
            elif p < 0.01:
                stars = "**"
            elif p < ALPHA:
                stars = "*"
            else:
                stars = ""
            labels.loc[row, col] = f"{r:.2f}{stars}"

    # hide the upper half of the heatmap, which mirrors the lower half
    hide = np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape, dtype=bool))
    plt.figure(figsize=(9, 7))
    sns.heatmap(corr, mask=hide, annot=labels, fmt="", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1,
                cbar_kws={"label": "Correlation (r)"})
    plt.title(f"Correlations Among Playoff Teams – {ERA_CHOICES[era_choice]} (n = {len(data)})\n"
              "* p < .05   ** p < .01   *** p < .001")
    plt.xlabel("Variable")
    plt.ylabel("Variable")
    plt.show()

    regular_season = ["Run differential per game", "Winning %", "Team ERA", "Home runs per game"]
    with_post = corr.loc[regular_season, "Postseason W%"]
    top = with_post.abs().idxmax()
    r_top = with_post[top]
    r_opp = corr.loc["Opponent W%", "Postseason W%"]
    r_rd_wp = corr.loc["Run differential per game", "Winning %"]

    display(Markdown(
        f"**Interpretation:** Among playoff teams ({ERA_CHOICES[era_choice].lower()}), the regular-season stat most "
        f"closely related to postseason winning % is **{top}** (r = {labels.loc[top, 'Postseason W%']}), "
        f"a {strength(r_top)} correlation – regular-season dominance only partly carries over to October. "
        f"Facing tougher opponents has a {strength(r_opp)} relationship with postseason W% "
        f"(r = {labels.loc['Opponent W%', 'Postseason W%']}). "
        f"The regular-season stats are also correlated **with each other** – run differential and winning % "
        f"have r = {r_rd_wp:.2f} – which is why adding more of them to the regression barely improves it."
    ))

run_corr("all")

Interpretation: Among playoff teams (all eras), the regular-season stat most closely related to postseason winning % is Winning % (r = 0.27***), a weak correlation – regular-season dominance only partly carries over to October. Facing tougher opponents has a weak relationship with postseason W% (r = -0.02). The regular-season stats are also correlated with each other – run differential and winning % have r = 0.79 – which is why adding more of them to the regression barely improves it.

6.5 Do wild cards win as often as division winners? (chi-square)¶

Question: Since wild cards were added in 1995, do wild card teams win the World Series (or reach it) as often as division winners?

Method: pd.crosstab counts the teams in each combination, and chi2_contingency compares those counts with what would be expected if entry type didn't matter. Cramér's V is the effect size (0 = no relationship, 1 = perfect).

Parameters: which – won the World Series (title) or reached it (pennant).

In [ ]:
CHI_OUTCOMES = {
    "title":   "Won the World Series",
    "pennant": "Reached the World Series",
}
WILD_CARD_START = 1995

def run_chisq(which=None):
    which = pick(CHI_OUTCOMES, "Compare division winners and wild cards on: ", which)
    out_label = CHI_OUTCOMES[which]

    data = analysis[analysis["yearID"] >= WILD_CARD_START].copy()

    data["Entry"] = np.where(data["DivWin"] == "Y", "Division winner", "Wild card")
    if which == "title":
        data["Result"] = np.where(data["outcome"] == "Champion", "Yes", "No")
    else:
        data["Result"] = np.where(data["outcome"] != "Lost earlier", "Yes", "No")

    observed = pd.crosstab(data["Entry"], data["Result"])[["Yes", "No"]]
    chi2, p, dof, expected = stats.chi2_contingency(observed)
    expected = pd.DataFrame(expected, index=observed.index, columns=observed.columns)

    n = observed.values.sum()
    # Cramér's V effect size: 0 = no relationship, 1 = perfect relationship
    cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * (min(observed.shape) - 1)))

    observed["Total"] = observed["Yes"] + observed["No"]
    observed["Rate"] = observed["Yes"] / observed["Total"]

    styled(observed, f"Observed counts: {out_label}", {"Yes": "{:.0f}", "No": "{:.0f}", "Total": "{:.0f}", "Rate": "{:.1%}"})
    styled(expected, "Expected counts if entry type didn't matter", "{:.1f}")
    test_table = pd.DataFrame({"Chi-square": [chi2], "df": [dof], "p-value": [p], "Cramér's V": [cramers_v]},
                              index=["Chi-square test"])
    styled(test_table, "Chi-square test of independence",
           {"Chi-square": "{:.3f}", "df": "{:.0f}", "p-value": "{:.4f}", "Cramér's V": "{:.3f}"})

    overall = observed["Yes"].sum() / observed["Total"].sum()
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    plt.bar(observed.index, observed["Rate"] * 100, color=["navy", "goldenrod"], label=out_label)
    for i, (rate, yes, total) in enumerate(zip(observed["Rate"], observed["Yes"], observed["Total"])):
        plt.text(i, rate * 100 + 0.5, f"{rate:.1%}\n({yes:.0f} of {total:.0f})", ha="center")
    plt.axhline(overall * 100, color="red", linestyle="--", label=f"All playoff teams ({overall:.1%})")
    plt.title(f"{out_label}: Division Winners vs. Wild Cards ({WILD_CARD_START}–{NEW_SEASON})\n"
              f"χ² = {chi2:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}, Cramér's V = {cramers_v:.2f}")
    plt.xlabel("How the team entered the playoffs")
    plt.ylabel("% of teams")
    plt.ylim(0, observed["Rate"].max() * 100 * 1.4)
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

    outcome_text = out_label[0].lower() + out_label[1:]
    note = ""
    if (expected < 5).values.any():
        note = " *Note: at least one expected count is below 5, so treat this p-value with caution.*"
    display(Markdown(
        f"**Interpretation:** {p_sentence(p, f'relationship between how a team entered the playoffs and whether it {outcome_text}')} "
        f"Division winners: {observed.loc['Division winner', 'Rate']:.1%}; wild cards: {observed.loc['Wild card', 'Rate']:.1%}. "
        f"Cramér's V = {cramers_v:.2f} ({size_label(cramers_v, (0.1, 0.3, 0.5))} association).{note}"
    ))

6.6 How often does the best team win?¶

Question: How often did the team with the best regular season win the World Series?

Steps: filter to seasons that had a champion → rank every team within its season with groupby + rank → filter to the #1 team and the champion → merge them into one row per season → summarize by era with groupby. This option uses all teams, not just playoff teams.

Parameters: rank_col – define "best" by record or by run differential.

In [ ]:
RANK_BY = {
    "win_pct":  "Best record (winning %)",
    "rd_per_g": "Best run differential per game",
}

def run_best_team(rank_col=None):
    rank_col = pick(RANK_BY, "Define 'best team' by: ", rank_col)
    rank_label = RANK_BY[rank_col]

    champion_years = po[po["outcome"] == "Champion"]["yearID"]
    seasons = teams[teams["yearID"].isin(champion_years)].copy()

    # rank every team within its own season (1 = best)
    seasons["mlb_rank"] = seasons.groupby("yearID")[rank_col].rank(ascending=False, method="min")

    best = seasons[seasons["mlb_rank"] == 1].drop_duplicates("yearID")
    best = best[["yearID", "teamID", "name"]].rename(columns={"teamID": "best_team", "name": "Best team"})

    champs = seasons[seasons["WSWin"] == "Y"]
    champs = champs[["yearID", "teamID", "name", "mlb_rank"]].rename(
        columns={"teamID": "champion", "name": "Champion", "mlb_rank": "Champion's MLB rank"})

    by_year = pd.merge(best, champs, on="yearID")
    by_year["best_won"] = by_year["best_team"] == by_year["champion"]
    by_year = pd.merge(by_year, po[["yearID", "era"]].drop_duplicates(), on="yearID")

    grouped = by_year.groupby("era", observed=True)
    summary = pd.DataFrame({
        "Seasons":                 grouped["best_won"].count(),
        "Best team won":           grouped["best_won"].sum(),
        "Best-team win rate":      grouped["best_won"].mean(),
        "Champion's avg MLB rank": grouped["Champion's MLB rank"].mean(),
    })
    styled(summary, f"Did the team with the {rank_label.lower()} win the World Series?",
           {"Seasons": "{:.0f}", "Best team won": "{:.0f}", "Best-team win rate": "{:.1%}",
            "Champion's avg MLB rank": "{:.1f}"})

    recent = by_year[["yearID", "Best team", "Champion", "Champion's MLB rank", "best_won"]].tail(8)
    recent["best_won"] = np.where(recent["best_won"], "Yes", "No")
    recent = recent.rename(columns={"yearID": "Season", "best_won": "Best team won?"}).set_index("Season")
    styled(recent, "Most recent seasons", {"Champion's MLB rank": "{:.0f}"})

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
    plt.bar(summary.index.astype(str), summary["Best-team win rate"] * 100, color="navy",
            label="Best team won the title")
    for i, (rate, won, n) in enumerate(zip(summary["Best-team win rate"], summary["Best team won"], summary["Seasons"])):
        plt.text(i, rate * 100 + 1, f"{rate:.0%}\n({won:.0f} of {n:.0f})", ha="center")
    overall = by_year["best_won"].mean()
    plt.axhline(overall * 100, color="red", linestyle="--", label=f"All seasons ({overall:.0%})")
    plt.title(f"How Often Did the Team With the {rank_label.split(' (')[0].title()} Win the World Series? "
              f"({START_YEAR}–{NEW_SEASON})")
    plt.xlabel("Playoff era")
    plt.ylabel("% of seasons")
    plt.ylim(0, max(summary["Best-team win rate"].max() * 100 * 1.3, 50))
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

    first_era, last_era = summary.index[0], summary.index[-1]
    first_rate = summary.loc[first_era, "Best-team win rate"]
    last_rate = summary.loc[last_era, "Best-team win rate"]
    low_era = summary["Best-team win rate"].idxmin()
    if last_rate > first_rate:
        trend = "higher"
    elif last_rate < first_rate:
        trend = "lower"
    else:
        trend = "the same"

    this_year = by_year[by_year["yearID"] == NEW_SEASON]
    note = ""
    if len(this_year) > 0 and this_year["best_won"].iloc[0]:
        note = f" In {NEW_SEASON}, the best team **did** win: the Brewers."

    display(Markdown(
        f"**Interpretation:** Across {len(by_year)} seasons, the team with the {rank_label.lower()} won the "
        f"World Series only **{overall:.0%}** of the time – most titles go to a team that wasn't the best in the regular season. "
        f"The rate was lowest in the {low_era} era ({summary.loc[low_era, 'Best-team win rate']:.0%}), and in the "
        f"{last_era} era it is {trend} than in {first_era} ({last_rate:.0%} vs. {first_rate:.0%}), although recent eras "
        f"have only a handful of seasons, so a single title changes the rate a lot.{note}"
    ))

7. Conclusion, limitations, and next steps¶

The 2026 Brewers rank among the most dominant World Series champions since 1969 – roughly a top-10 team – but not the single greatest. They were elite in both the regular season and the postseason, and they won in an unusual way.

Regular season: elite, and earned¶

  • Best record in baseball (103-59). Since 1969, the team with the best record has won the World Series only 28% of the time (Section 6.6), so finishing first and winning the title is uncommon.
  • #8 of 55 champions in run differential (87th percentile), just ahead of the 1976 Cincinnati Reds (Section 5.1).
  • The record wasn't luck. Run differential predicted 102.5 wins; they won 103 (Section 5.2).

Postseason: among the best¶

  • 11-2 (.846), 87th percentile among champions – tied with the 2022 Astros for the best postseason record of the 12-team era.
  • Compared with those Astros, the Brewers won by a larger margin (+2.00 vs. +1.31 runs per game) against tougher opponents (.595 vs. .568 regular-season winning %).
  • Their margin ranks #13 of 55 – decisive, but short of the 2007 Red Sox (+3.79) and 1970 Orioles (+3.75).
  • The regular season predicted a postseason winning % of about .45; they played .846 (Section 6.3).
  • Combining postseason winning %, run margin, and opponent strength, their run ranks #5 of 31 among champions since 1995 (Section 5.3). Before 1995 a champion needed only 7–8 postseason wins, so short sweeps inflate older teams' numbers; comparing only champions since 1995, who all had to win at least three series, is the fairer test. Against every champion since 1969, they rank #9 of 55.

What made them different¶

  • They beat the typical champion on 6 of 7 measures – but ranked in the 4th percentile in home runs, one of the least powerful champions in the dataset. They won through overall run prevention and run differential, not the long ball.
  • The 2025 Brewers also had baseball's best record and lost in the playoffs. In 2026 they turned the same regular-season dominance into a title.

The bigger lesson¶

Run differential explains 88% of regular-season winning, but regular-season stats explain only about 6% of postseason winning (Sections 5.2 and 6.3). Champions and World Series losers were statistically indistinguishable (Section 6.2), and wild cards won titles about as often as division winners (Section 6.5). October is highly unpredictable – which makes a run as complete as Milwaukee's 2026 season stand out even more.

Limitations¶

  • Postseason samples are small (11–13 games for a modern champion), so postseason rankings are less stable than regular-season ones.
  • The 1981 strike-shortened split season and the 60-game 2020 season were excluded from the statistical tests; 1994 had no postseason.
  • The 2022+ era includes only five seasons, so era comparisons involving it should be read with caution.
  • Lahman has no game-by-game scores, so "margin" is the average run differential across all postseason games, not only wins.

Next steps¶

  • Extend the window before 1969 to compare pre-divisional champions, who went straight to the World Series, with champions under today's multi-round format.
  • Add game-level data (e.g., Retrosheet game logs) to measure margin in wins only, one-run-game records, and series-by-series opponent quality.
  • Model postseason outcomes at the series level (e.g., logistic regression on the seed and run-differential gap between opponents) instead of a season-level winning %.

Appendix: Interactive explorer¶

Every analysis above is also available through a text menu. A dictionary maps each number to its analysis function, so adding an analysis takes one line. Run the cell below, then call menu(); each option asks for its own parameters, and q quits.

In [ ]:
MENU = {
    "1": ("T-test: champions vs. other playoff teams",                   run_ttest),
    "2": ("ANOVA: compare outcomes or eras (with Tukey post-hoc)",        run_anova),
    "3": ("Regression: was the record earned? / can it predict October?", run_regression),
    "4": ("Chi-square: do wild cards win as often as division winners?", run_chisq),
    "5": ("Data management: did the best team win the title?",           run_best_team),
    "6": ("Correlation heatmap",                                         run_corr),
    "7": ("How do the 2026 Brewers rank among champions?",               run_brewers),
    "8": ("Rank the 2026 Brewers' postseason run among all champions",   rank_postseason_runs),
}


def menu():
    """Show the menu, run the chosen analysis, and repeat until the user quits."""
    while True:
        print("\n=== 2026 Brewers & MLB Champions Explorer ===")
        for key, (label, _) in MENU.items():
            print(f"  {key}. {label}")
        print("  q. Quit")
        choice = input("Choose an option: ").strip().lower()
        if choice == "q":
            print("Thanks for exploring!")
            break
        if choice in MENU:
            # call the function stored for this menu choice
            MENU[choice][1]()
        else:
            print("Invalid choice – please enter 1-8 or q.")
